module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 373

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped Nat

namespace Erdos373

/--
Let `S` be the set of non-trivial solutions to the equation `n! = a₁! ··· aₖ!`
such that `a₁ ≥ ... ≥ aₖ` and `n-1 > a₁`.
-/
abbrev S : Set (ℕ × List ℕ) :=
  {(n, l) | n ! = (l.map Nat.factorial).prod ∧ l.Pairwise (· ≥ ·)
    ∧ l.headI < (n - 1 : ℕ) ∧ ∀ a ∈ l, 1 < a }

/--
Show that the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has
only finitely many solutions.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_373 : S.Finite := by
  sorry

/--
Show that if `P(n(n+1)) / log n → ∞` where `P(m)` denotes the largest prime factor of `m`, then
the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has only
finitely many solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_373.variants.of_limit
    (H : Filter.atTop.Tendsto (fun (n : ℕ) => (n*(n+1)).maxPrimeFac / (n : ℝ).log) Filter.atTop) :
    S.Finite := by
  sorry

-- Formalisation note: at the time of writing, the website states "Erdős proved that this problem
-- would also follow from showing that $P(n(n - 1)) > 4\log n$". This is slightly unclear
-- as to which $n$ is meant here, as for example the inequality fails for $n = 4$.
-- The referenced material (Theorem 2 of https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1976-39.pdf), shows
-- that no non-trivial solutions hold for any `n` with `n > n_0` and `P(n(n - 1)) > 4 log n`.
-- So for finiteness, it is enough to assume the inequality holds for sufficiently large `n`.
/--
Show that if `P(n(n−1)) > 4 log n` for large enough `n`, where `P(m)` denotes the
largest prime factor of `m`, then the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with
`n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has only finitely many solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_373.variants.of_lower_bound
    (H : ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, 4*(n : ℝ).log < (n*(n-1 : ℕ)).maxPrimeFac) :
    S.Finite := by
  sorry

/--
Hickerson conjectured the largest solution the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with
`n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, is `16!=14!5!2!`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_373.variants.maximal_solution :
    (16, [14, 5, 2]) ∈ S ∧ ∀ s ∈ S, s.fst ≤ 16 := by
  sorry

/--
Surányi was the first to conjecture that the only non-trivial solution to `a!b!=n!`
is `6!7!=10!`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_373.variants.suranyi :
    {(n, a, b) : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | n ! = a ! * b ! ∧ 1 < n ∧ 1 < a ∧ 1 < b ∧ b ≤ a ∧ a + 1 ≠ n}
      = {(10, 7, 6)} := by
  sorry

end Erdos373

findings.description: The docstrings of `erdos_373`, `erdos_373.variants.of_limit`, `erdos_373.variants.of_lower_bound` and `erdos_373.variants.maximal_solution` give the side condition as "with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`". They drop the source's final "≥ 2". The `S` docstring likewise lists only `a₁ ≥ ... ≥ aₖ` and `n-1 > a₁`. Read literally, the docstring problem is trivially false: padding 10! = 7!6! with factors 1! (or 0!) gives infinitely many solutions. The Lean definition `S` does contain `∀ a ∈ l, 1 < a`, so every formal statement is correct. Only the prose is off.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/373 (LaTeX source): "Show that the equation \[n! = a_1!a_2!\cdots a_k!,\] with $n-1>a_1\geq a_2\geq \cdots \geq a_k\geq 2$, has only finitely many solutions." Erdős [Er76d] (users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1976-39.pdf, p. 40), eq. (28): n! = ∏ a_i!, n−2 ≥ a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ … ≥ 2.
findings.suggested_fix: Write the condition as $n-1 > a_1 \geq a_2 \geq \cdots \geq a_k \geq 2$ in the docstrings of erdos_373, of_limit, of_lower_bound and maximal_solution, and mention $a_k \geq 2$ in the docstring of `S`.

reformulations.difference: A solution is encoded as a pair (n, l : List ℕ). The condition n−1 > a_1 is written `l.headI < (n - 1 : ℕ)`, which uses the default `headI [] = 0` and truncated subtraction. The ordering a_1 ≥ … ≥ a_k is `l.Pairwise (· ≥ ·)`, and k is not fixed.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a nonempty list, `headI` is a_1 and n ≥ 1 is forced, so `n - 1` is honest. For the empty list, n! = 1 forces n ≤ 1, so n - 1 = 0 and `0 < 0` fails; empty lists never occur. k = 1 is impossible (a_1! = n! with 2 ≤ a_1 < n−1). A sorted list represents each multiset exactly once. For fixed n there are finitely many lists (entries in [2, n−2], length ≤ log₂ n!). So S.Finite is exactly 'finitely many solutions'. Proved in Lean: (n, l) ∈ S ↔ ∃ a t, l = a :: t ∧ n! = ∏ (l.map factorial) ∧ l.Pairwise (· ≥ ·) ∧ a + 1 < n ∧ ∀ x ∈ l, 1 < x.

reformulations.difference: Hickerson's conjecture as posed says the only non-trivial solutions are 9! = 7!3!3!2!, 10! = 7!6!, 10! = 7!5!3! and 16! = 14!5!2!. The Lean says only that (16, [14,5,2]) ∈ S and that every s ∈ S has s.1 ≤ 16 (the docstring's 'largest solution').
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An exhaustive #eval search (complete search with divisibility pruning) over every n ≤ 40 finds exactly (9,[7,3,3,2]), (10,[7,6]), (10,[7,5,3]) and (16,[14,5,2]); each passes S's decidable predicate, and `decide` confirms membership. So S ∩ {n ≤ 16} is exactly the four listed solutions. Hence '∀ s ∈ S, s.1 ≤ 16' holds iff S equals those four, and the first conjunct is a true fact. This was checked by computation, not proved as a kernel ↔.

reformulations.difference: 'Non-trivial solution of a!b! = n!' is encoded as 1 < a, 1 < b, a + 1 ≠ n (with the redundant 1 < n). The symmetry is broken by b ≤ a, so the answer set is {(10,7,6)} rather than both orders of 6!7! = 10!.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Erdős [Er76d] calls a solution of n! = a!b! trivial when n = a+1 = b!. Proved in Lean: a + 1 = n together with n! = a!·b! forces n = b!, and the family (b!, b!−1, b) satisfies the equation. So a + 1 ≠ n excludes exactly that family. The conditions 1 < a and 1 < b exclude the degenerate 0!/1! factors. Under b ≤ a, the swapped trivial family b = n−1, a! = n would force a = b = n−1 and n = (n−1)!, which has no solution with a ≥ 2. The #eval search for n ≤ 200 returns exactly {(10,7,6)}.

reformulations.difference: The source says only that the problem 'would also follow from showing that P(n(n−1)) > 4 log n', without quantifying n. The Lean assumes the inequality for all sufficiently large n (∀ᶠ n in atTop).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Theorem 2 of [Er76d] (p. 28, proof on p. 40) says: assume P(n(n−1)) > 4 log n; then for n > n₀, (7) n! = ∏aᵢ! has only trivial solutions, with (28) taken under n−2 ≥ a₁ ≥ … ≥ 2, i.e. exactly S's constraints. So an eventual lower bound gives S.Finite. A 'for all n' reading would make the hypothesis false (for n = 4, P(12) = 3 < 4 log 4, checked in Lean) and the implication vacuous, so the eventual reading is the faithful one. `of_limit` follows from it by the shift n ↦ n−1.

review.notes:
The file is faithful to erdosproblems.com/373 and to Erdős [Er76d]. The only defect found is a docstring slip: the docstrings drop "≥ 2".

Categories match the source. The main problem, Hickerson's conjecture and Surányi's conjecture are open (erdosproblems.com shows OPEN, page last edited 29 Jan 2026; the teorth database also says open). The two conditional variants are correctly tagged solved: Erdős's Theorem 2 proves `of_lower_bound`, and `of_limit` follows from it by shifting n to n−1.

The hypotheses of the conditional variants are open, not known to be false. Problem 368 records only F(n) ≫ (log log n)²/log log log n and conjectures F(n) ≫ (log n)², so neither statement is known to be vacuous.

Lean checks run in /workspace/review:
- `#print` and `#check` on every declaration show the expected elaboration: casts sit on the whole `maxPrimeFac`, and `n - 1` is ℕ subtraction.
- `decide` confirms membership of all four Hickerson solutions in `S`, and rejects a false one (the harness sanity check).
- Proved lemmas: the characterization of `S` membership, and exclusion of the empty list.
- Proved lemmas for the Surányi trivial family: a + 1 = n with the equation forces n = b!, and that family satisfies the equation.
- Exhaustive `#eval` searches: the solutions with n ≤ 40, and the Surányi set with n ≤ 200.

Access notes: erdosproblems.com is behind a Cloudflare challenge, so I read it through the r.jina.ai reader proxy. web.archive.org was unreachable. The 1976 Erdős PDF is a scan and was OCR'd page by page. I did not consult [ErGr80, p.70], [Er97e, p.537], Guy B23 or Luca 2007; they were not needed, since erdosproblems.com and [Er76d] settle every declaration.
